coach_says: Your bishop on e6 was already attacking c4, and nothing defends that pawn, so Bxc4 simply wins it. Instead d5 opens the centre while your king is still on e8: after exd5 cxd5 d4 White hits e5 while c4 presses on d5, and your centre comes apart. Before pushing a pawn, check whether one of your pieces can just take something for free.
concept: missed a free pawn on c4
also: opening the centre with the king uncastled

coach_says: Your e5 pawn was shielding the c7-h2 diagonal. After e6, Qc7 attacks your rook on f4, which nothing defends, and if the rook steps away Qxh2+ and Qh1 is mate because the g4 knight also hits h2. Then g5 attacks the stuck rook and you have to give it up for the knight. Before pushing a pawn, ask which lines it opens for your opponent; d3, keeping e5 and opening your bishop, was the solid move.
concept: pawn push opened a diagonal onto the rook

coach_says: Your knight on e7 was pinned by the rook on e1, and your king on e8 was the only piece guarding it. Castling queenside took the king away, so Rxe7 just wins a knight. Before moving a piece, check what it was defending; Kd8 or Kf8 unpins while keeping the king next to e7.
concept: castled away the knight's only defender

coach_says: Your king has no escape square and nothing guards your back rank, so Rc8 pins the d8 knight to your king. Nc6 tries to get out, but d5 hits the knight and it has no good square: Nd8 walks back into the Rc8 pin, and Nxe5 runs into Rc8+ Bf8 Nxe5. Fix the real problem first: Kf8 and Ke8 brings the king over to protect the knight and ends the back-rank trouble.

Your c6 knight had to move, but on b4 it is guarded only by the c5 bishop while White's queen on d2 attacks it. White takes on e7 first, then d4 attacks the bishop, and Black can't keep the bishop safe and the knight defended at the same time, so material goes. Nd4 was the natural square: central and protected by both the bishop and the e5 pawn.

Kf6 is a reasonable move and you are still better, but your rook on c8 is stuck guarding c7. Re8 goes after the e4 pawn, which White can't easily defend, and if White pushes e5 the pawns come off and your rook becomes the active one. In rook endings an active rook that attacks pawns is usually worth more than a quiet king move.

After Nc7+ your a8 rook is in danger, but your b2 bishop is attacking White's a1 rook, so you can win material back. Kd7 attacks the forking knight: if White saves the rook with Rab1 you just take on c7, so White has to take a8, you take a1, and the knight on a8 is trapped. After Ke7 White has time for Rab1, saving the rook with an attack on your bishop, and then picks up a8 and b7.
concept: attack the forking knight with the king

coach_says: Black was threatening Qb6+, hitting your king on f2 along the open diagonal, and Nf4 does nothing about it. Worse, the knight leaves e2, so Black's e8 rook now faces your e1 rook, and the knight on f4 can be taken by the h6 bishop: after Qb6+ d4 Rxe1 Kxe1 Bxf4 gxf4 Black's queen gets into b2. f4 shuts the h6 bishop out and keeps the knight shielding the e-file. When your king stands on an open diagonal, look for the checks against it first.
concept: missed the threat Qb6+ on f2

coach_says: Your g4 bishop looks like it pins the f3 knight, but only the e2 bishop stands behind it, and if you take that White just recaptures with the queen. So the knight is free to move, and after e5 Nxe5 takes your pawn and attacks g4 too. Bxf3 first gets rid of the knight that was attacking both d4 and e5.

Black's knight on d4 wants to jump to f3. From there it covers g1, and with the queen on h3 and the pawn on h2, Qg4 followed by Qg1+ Rxg1 hxg1=Q is mate. f5 does nothing about it. f2-f3 takes the f3 square away from the knight; deal with the threat to your king before pushing your own attack.
concept: missed the knight jump to f3

coach_says: After gxf5 the g-file is open and White's bishop on h6 already sits next to your king. b5 ignores that: Rg1+ Kh8 Bg7+ Kg8 Bxf6+ Kf8 Rg8+ and Qg4 ends in mate on g7. Kh8 followed by Rg8 puts your own rook on the open file and stops it all. When a file opens towards your king, get a rook onto it before doing anything else.

Your king on h1 is boxed in by Black's pawn on h2 and queen on h3, and the d4 knight is one jump from f3, where it helps mate you on g1. Bxd4 removes that knight before it gets there. cxd6 wins a pawn but gives Black time for Nf3, and the attack crashes through. When enemy pieces are right next to your king, remove the most dangerous attacker before grabbing material.
concept: missed the knight jump to f3

coach_says: You are a piece down, so you need moves that make threats. Rfe1 attacks the queen with gain of time and puts your rook on the e-file, where Black's king still sits; Qc7 going after b7 was also active. Be3 is a quiet retreat that lets Black play e5 and get organised.
also: rook to the file of the uncastled king

coach_says: Both your knight and your bishop could take on c4, so ask what happens after dxc4. With Bxc4 dxc4 your d2 knight recaptures, you win a pawn and get a strong knight aiming at d6. After Nxc4 dxc4 you can't safely take back, because Bxc4 runs into Qxd4 hitting the bishop. You're still winning, but take with the piece that leaves another one ready to recapture.

Your knight on f6 blocks your g7 bishop, and on that long diagonal stand White's d4 knight, the c3 knight and the a1 rook. Nfd5 opens the bishop and attacks the c3 knight, which has no defender, so White has to spend time while his king is still in the centre. Castling is a normal move, but it gives White time for Bb2 to cover the diagonal; when your opponent is behind in development, use the tempo first.
concept: unblock the bishop on the long diagonal

coach_says: Taking with the h-pawn opens the h-file, and then your h1 rook and d3 bishop both hit h7, which only the h8 rook defends, so Rxh7 is coming and wins a pawn. fxg3 is playable, but before recapturing, ask which file each capture opens for your rooks.
also: attack h7 with rook and bishop

coach_says: You are a piece down, so you need moves that gain time. White's queen on g5 is a target: h6 and then g5 push it back, and the g-pawn can go on to g4 against the f3 knight and the king on f2. Bb4 only pins a knight against a bishop and gives White time for Bd3 and to tidy up.
also: attack the exposed king on f2

coach_says: Your king is still on e1 and your knights aren't out yet, while Black's c5 bishop aims at e3. d4 hits that bishop with gain of time, blocks its diagonal and opens lines for your pieces in the centre. Bc3 moves an already developed piece again and lets Black carry on developing.
also: develop before moving a piece twice

coach_says: Your d7 bishop was blocking the d-file. Once it takes on c6, White's d1 rook looks straight through your d6 pawn at your queen, so d6 can't really defend e5 and Nxe5 wins a pawn. bxc6 keeps the bishop as a shield, keeps d5 covered by a pawn and opens the b-file towards White's king on c1.
concept: recapture opened a pin on d6
also: open the b-file against the castled king

coach_says: In this Traxler line the point is Bxf2+ straight away: White's king has to move (Kxf2 Nxe4+ and Qh4 gives you a strong attack) and can never castle. After Qe7 White grabs the h8 rook and can still castle to safety, so your attack loses its target. In sharp gambits, play the forcing move first, before your opponent gets his king out.
